concepts.title: What is a Social Institution?
concepts.definition: A social institution is a stable cluster of norms, roles and procedures organised around a basic social need -- family for kinship and care, economy for livelihood, polity for power, religion for meaning. Institutions look natural because they have always been there, yet each is a human construction that varies across societies and changes over time.
concepts.key_idea: Institutions are society's durable answers to recurring needs -- made by people, mistaken for nature.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesy103.txt lines 15-130 (introduction, why study institutions, institutions as sets of norms and roles meeting basic needs, examples of family economy polity religion)
question_patterns: define a social institution and give examples
in class 11 understanding social institutions: why are institutions said to be humanly constructed
how do institutions differ from informal groups
what basic needs do the major institutions serve
why do institutions appear natural to their members
explain how institutions constrain individual behaviour

solution_steps.explain: Every institution answers a recurring collective need -- reproduction, subsistence, order, meaning.
The institution packages that answer as norms, roles and statuses reproduced across generations.
Cross-cultural variation shows each institutional form is historical, not natural -- and therefore changeable.

worked_examples.q: Which institution is organised around kinship and care?

concepts.title: Family, Marriage and Kinship
concepts.definition: The family is the institutional core of kinship -- the network of relationships traced through blood and marriage. Forms vary: nuclear and joint households, monogamy, polygyny and polyandry, patrilocal and matrilocal residence. Marriage rules of endogamy and exogamy decide who one may marry, and descent rules decide who one belongs to.
concepts.key_idea: Marriage writes the rules of alliance; descent writes the rules of belonging -- family forms are many, not one.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesy103.txt lines 130-280 (family marriage kinship, nuclear and extended family, monogamy polygyny polyandry, endogamy exogamy, patriliny matriliny, rules of residence)
question_patterns: distinguish nuclear family from extended family
in class 11 understanding social institutions: define endogamy and exogamy with examples
what are polygyny and polyandry
explain patriliny and matriliny with indian examples
how do rules of residence affect family structure
why is marriage called an alliance between groups not just individuals

solution_steps.explain: Count the married couples and generations sharing residence: one couple makes a nuclear family, more make extended or joint families.
Endogamy requires marrying within the group -- caste for instance; exogamy requires marrying outside -- the village or gotra.
Patriliny traces descent through fathers, matriliny through mothers; residence after marriage may be with either side or neither.

worked_examples.q: Marriage within one's own group is called what?

concepts.title: Power, Authority and the State
concepts.definition: Power is the ability to make others do what one wants; authority is power accepted as legitimate. Max Weber's classic types -- traditional, charismatic and legal-rational -- name the grounds on which obedience is claimed. Modern states monopolise legitimate violence within a territory and organise authority through law and bureaucracy.
concepts.key_idea: Power persuades or forces; authority persuades because it is believed right -- legitimacy is the difference.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesy103.txt lines 280-400 (power authority and the state, weber's three types of authority, legitimacy, modern state and bureaucracy)
question_patterns: distinguish power from authority with examples
in class 11 understanding social institutions: explain weber's three types of authority
what makes the modern state's authority legal rational
why does the state claim a monopoly of legitimate violence
can charisma become traditional authority
how does bureaucracy serve the modern state

solution_steps.explain: A robber exercises power; an elected government exercises authority -- the latter is obeyed as rightful.
Traditional authority rests on custom, charismatic on a leader's exceptional qualities, legal-rational on impersonal rules and offices.
The modern state grounds itself in legal-rational authority, staffed by bureaucracy and claiming sole right to legitimate coercion.

worked_examples.q: Power accepted as legitimate is called what?

concepts.title: Economy, Religion and Education as Institutions
concepts.definition: The economy institutionalises the production and distribution of livelihood -- from hunting-gathering through agrarian to industrial and knowledge systems. Religion institutionalises the sacred: beliefs, rituals and organisations that bind communities and sanctify norms. Education institutionalises the transmission of knowledge and values, both preserving culture and equipping change.
concepts.key_idea: Livelihood, meaning and learning each have their institution -- economy, religion, education -- shaping and shaped by the rest.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesy103.txt lines 400-500 (economic institutions, division of labour, religion as institution, ritual and sacred, education and transmission of culture)
question_patterns: describe the economy as a social institution
in class 11 understanding social institutions: how does religion function as a social institution
what is the role of education in transmitting culture

how do rituals sustain community solidarity

solution_steps.explain: Societies organise livelihood differently -- hunting, farming, industry, services -- with each division of labour reshaping social bonds.
Sacred beliefs and rituals regularise the unexplained and consecrate moral rules, binding participants into moral communities.
Schools pass on inherited knowledge and simultaneously prepare members for new roles -- conservation and change together.

worked_examples.q: Which institution organises the production and distribution of livelihood?

worked_examples.question_pattern: In a South Indian matrilineal community, children belong to the mother's house and a man's heirs are his sister's children. Identify the descent, residence and marriage rules at work.

solution_template.explain: Inheritance and belonging through the mother's line marks matriliny.
Where the wife remains in her mother's house with her children, residence is marilocal/matri-centered rather than patrilocal.
Alliance links two houses rather than transferring the bride, showing marriage as inter-group arrangement within kinship structure.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A hereditary king rules by custom, a rebel saint draws devoted crowds, and an income tax officer issues a notice. Match each to Weber's types of authority.

solution_template.explain: Obedience flows from age-old custom -- traditional authority.
Followers respond to extraordinary personal qualities -- charismatic authority.
The notice binds because it issues from an office under impersonal law -- legal-rational authority, the modern state's mode.
